displayQuote: Hell hath no fury like a woman scorned

meta.title: Who really said "Hell hath no fury like a woman scorned"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: It's a paraphrase of William Congreve's 1697 play The Mourning Bride. He wrote “has,” not “hath” — which is why it's so often mistaken for Shakespeare.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Hell hath no fury like a woman scorned'?
meta.ogDescription: Congreve's real line from The Mourning Bride (1697) — and why the famous version is a reworded proverb, not his exact words.

answer.label: A paraphrase of William Congreve
answer.sourceLine: The thought — and very nearly the words — are genuinely Congreve’s, from his 1697 tragedy The Mourning Bride, where the captive queen Zara declares: “Heav’n has no Rage, like Love to Hatred turn’d, / Nor Hell a Fury, like a Woman scorn’d.” The familiar one-liner is a later compression: it drops the first line, and the archaic “hath” (which Congreve never wrote — he wrote “has”) is what makes so many people mistake it for Shakespeare.

source.heading: The real line

docMeta.dd: Zara, a captive queen, in Act III
“Nor Hell a Fury, like a Woman scorn’d” (not “hath”)

source.excerpt:
Heav’n has no Rage, like Love to Hatred turn’d,
Nor Hell a Fury, like a Woman scorn’d.
trail: Congreve’s original couplet appears in Act III, spoken by Zara, in the 1697 text on Wikisource ↗.
Wikipedia’s entry on the play ↗ confirms the wording, the speaker Zara, and that the line is now usually paraphrased as “Hell hath no fury like a woman scorned.”
The compressed form “Hell has no Fury like a Woman scorn’d” is documented circulating as a saying by 1726 in Nicholas Amhurst’s Terræ-Filius, per Word Histories ↗.
source.excerptNote: The couplet as printed in 1697 — the popular saying keeps only the second line and swaps Congreve’s “has” for the archaic “hath.”
source.rightsNote: The line comes from The Mourning Bride, first performed and printed in 1697 — centuries before the 1931 U.S. copyright cutoff — so Congreve’s text is firmly in the public domain. The familiar paraphrase is an anonymous proverb of the same public-domain lineage.

author.name: William Congreve
author.heading: William Congreve
author.bio: William Congreve was the leading comic playwright of the English Restoration, celebrated for Love for Love (1695) and The Way of the World (1700). His single tragedy, The Mourning Bride (1697), was a huge stage success and is now remembered almost entirely for two lines it gave the language: this one and “Musick has Charms to soothe a savage Breast.” He largely gave up the theatre in his thirties and lived out his life on official sinecures and literary friendships.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: Almost everyone quotes this line slightly wrong, and many credit the wrong author entirely.

items.why: The archaic “hath” makes it sound Shakespearean, and it is routinely attributed to him — but Shakespeare died in 1616, over 80 years before Congreve wrote the play. The word doesn’t even appear in Congreve’s text; it crept in as the saying spread, as Word Histories documents ↗.
Congreve wrote “has,” not “hath,” and his line is one half of a two-line couplet beginning “Heav’n has no Rage, like Love to Hatred turn’d.” The stand-alone proverb is a paraphrase, per Wikipedia ↗.

A very similar sentiment appeared a year earlier in Cibber’s comedy Love’s Last Shift (1696) — “no Fiend in Hell can match the fury of a disappointed Woman” — so Congreve was working a theme already in the air, as noted by Word Histories ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentiment is genuinely Congreve’s, from The Mourning Bride (1697) — but he wrote a two-line couplet with “has,” and the snappy “hath” version is a later, anonymous paraphrase, not Shakespeare and not verbatim Congreve, per the primary text ↗.

context.heading: Why it stuck
lead: Congreve’s only tragedy was a sensation in 1697, and its most memorable moment is Zara’s vow of revenge. The couplet distils a whole revenge-tragedy tradition into two balanced lines — heaven’s rage set against hell’s fury — and the second half proved so quotable that it detached from the play and became a stand-alone proverb within a generation.

As it spread by ear rather than by the page, the line got smoother and older-sounding: the couplet’s first line fell away, “has” hardened into the biblical-sounding “hath,” and the result now reads to most people as timeless folk wisdom — or as Shakespeare.
context.pull: Congreve wrote “has.” The proverb we quote wrote itself.
